narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Born from the 1804 Revolution, this dance transformed the rigid European contredanse into a Haitian expression named after the elite Carabinier rifle regiments of the new army.
This is Karabinye. Early 19th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (tytB6vck7B0)
Title card: Karabinye · Haiti · Early 19th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Karabinye originated in Haiti immediately following the Revolution of 1804.
It was named after the Carabinier rifle regiments of the Haitian army.
The dance evolved from the kontradans (Haitian contredanse) and is recognized as a precursor to the Haitian méringue.
on_screen: Map: Haiti · Caribbean
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Karabinye served as a celebratory social dance for the newly independent Haitian population.
It carries a meaning of national identity and cultural synthesis, marking the transition from colonial subjects to an independent people with their own distinct ballroom traditions.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Karabinye is a couples dance that utilizes 'figures' derived from European social dances like the quadrille and lancers.
While specific step-by-step technical descriptions are not detailed in the sources, it is characterized by its evolution from a collective figure dance into a more localized partner form.
It incorporates the rhythmic and physical influences of the Kongo-Haitian traditions, likely involving more fluid torso movement than its European counterparts.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music of the Karabinye is a hybrid form that accompanies the dance's transition from contredanse to méringue.

While specific instrumentation is not listed in the sources, the style is defined by the blending of European melodic structures with African (specifically Kongo) rhythmic patterns including the banboula.
A blend of European melodic figures from the contredanse with the rhythmic drive of the banboula and kalenda.
